title: Measuring Angles Grade 4: Protractor Steps, Angle Types + Free Quiz
meta_title: Measuring Angles Grade 4: Protractor Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: Learn measuring angles grade 4 the easy way: name acute, right, obtuse and straight angles, read a protractor correctly, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Most Grade 4 mistakes with a protractor come from reading the wrong scale. Here is how I teach measuring angles in degrees, naming them by size, and drawing them — with a quick quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 4 child a protractor and ask them to measure a 40° angle, and about half the class will confidently write 140°. They lined up the vertex fine — they just read the wrong row of numbers. That single slip is the heart of what makes measuring angles grade 4 tricky, and it is completely fixable once children understand that an angle is measured in degrees, that a protractor has two scales for a reason, and that the size of the angle tells you which scale to trust.

In this guide I will walk through what a degree actually is, how to name angles by their size, the exact steps for measuring with a protractor, and how to draw an angle of your own. Grab a protractor, a sharp pencil and a ruler — this is a hands-on topic and reading about it only gets you halfway.

What a degree means

An angle measures a turn, and we measure that turn in degrees, written with a small circle: 90°. A full turn all the way around is 360°, half a turn is 180°, and a quarter turn — the square corner you see on a book or a window — is 90°. That quarter turn is the anchor. If a Grade 4 child can picture a right angle as a perfect corner, everything else is measured against it: smaller than a corner, bigger than a corner, or a dead-straight line.

Naming angles by their size

Before touching a protractor, children should be able to sort angles by eye. NCERT introduces four names in Grade 4, and I teach them strictly by degree range so there is no guesswork.

Angle typeSize in degreesEveryday example
AcuteLess than 90°A slightly open pair of scissors
RightExactly 90°The corner of a notebook
ObtuseBetween 90° and 180°A reclining chair back
StraightExactly 180°A flat, open ruler

A memory hook my students like: ‘acute’ angles are the small, cute ones. It sounds silly, and that is exactly why it sticks. The one children confuse most is obtuse versus straight — remind them that a straight angle is a perfectly flat line, so anything with even a slight bend is obtuse, not straight.

Right angles hiding in shapes

Right angles are everywhere in the shapes Grade 4 already knows. A square has four of them, a rectangle has four, and a right-angled triangle has exactly one. Ask a child to hunt for square corners around the room — door frames, tiles, the edge of a table — and the idea of 90° stops being abstract. Counting right angles in shapes is also a favourite exam question, so it is worth the practice.

How to measure an angle with a protractor

Here is the routine I drill until it becomes automatic. Say it out loud the first few times.

  • Centre on the vertex. Put the small hole or cross-mark in the middle of the protractor exactly on the corner point of the angle.
  • Line up the zero line. Rotate the protractor so one arm of the angle runs straight along the 0° line (the base line), not the bottom edge of the plastic.
  • Follow the second arm. Look at where the other arm crosses the curved scale.
  • Read the correct scale. Start counting from the 0° you lined up on. If the arm you started from was on the outer 0, read the outer numbers; if it was the inner 0, read the inner numbers.

The last step is where the 40°-versus-140° error lives. My fix is simple: before reading any number, decide whether the angle is acute or obtuse. If it clearly looks smaller than a square corner, the answer must be under 90° — so if the scale is offering you 140°, you know instantly to switch scales. That quick sanity check catches almost every misread.

How to draw an angle you are given

Measuring and drawing are two halves of the same skill. To draw, say, a 65° angle:

  • Draw a straight base line with a ruler and mark a point for the vertex at one end.
  • Place the protractor centre on that point and the zero line along the base line.
  • Count from 0° up to 65° on the correct scale and make a small dot.
  • Take the protractor away and join the vertex to your dot with a ruler.

Drawing forces children to choose the right scale themselves rather than just reading one, which is why I get more mileage out of ‘draw a 110° angle’ than out of ten more measuring questions.

A realistic practice routine

Angles reward short, frequent sessions with real tools over long ones on a screen. What works for the parents I know: two days naming angles by eye from pictures, two days measuring drawn angles, and one day drawing angles to a given size. Keep a genuine protractor in the pencil box — the printed ones in some workbooks are just distorted enough to teach the wrong reading, which is a caveat worth knowing.

One honest trade-off: do not rush a child onto exact readings before the acute/obtuse sorting is solid. A child who can estimate that an angle is ‘about 50°, definitely acute’ will self-correct a protractor slip. A child who only knows how to read numbers off plastic will trust whatever the scale says, wrong scale and all.

Test what your child has learned

Below is a short, free quiz on exactly these ideas — naming angles by size, reading the protractor and spotting right angles in shapes. Let your child try it, then talk through the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions on lines and angles with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Measuring Angles Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on naming angles, reading a protractor and right angles in shapes. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 4 angles: types, degrees and the protractor

questions.q: An angle that measures exactly 90° is called a...
questions.explanation: A right angle is exactly 90° — the square corner you see on a notebook.

questions.q: Which of these is an acute angle?
questions.explanation: An acute angle is less than 90°, so 45° is acute. The others are obtuse, right and straight.

questions.q: An angle of 130° is best described as...
questions.explanation: 130° is between 90° and 180°, so it is an obtuse angle.
A straight angle is a flat line, which is half a full turn: 180°.

questions.q: When measuring with a protractor, the centre point must sit on the...
questions.explanation: The centre mark of the protractor goes exactly on the vertex — the corner point where the two arms meet.

questions.q: How many right angles does a rectangle have?
questions.explanation: Every rectangle has four square corners, so it has four right angles.

questions.q: You measure an angle that clearly looks smaller than a square corner, and the scale shows either 35° or 145°. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: An angle smaller than a right angle must be under 90°, so the correct reading is 35°. This check stops the wrong-scale mistake.

questions.q: Which pair of angle names is in order from smallest to largest?
questions.explanation: Acute (under 90°), then right (90°), then obtuse (over 90°) is the correct order by size.

faq.q: What angles should a Grade 4 child know?
faq.a: Four types by size: acute (less than 90°), right (exactly 90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°) and straight (exactly 180°). They should also measure and draw angles with a protractor in degrees.

faq.q: Why does my child keep reading the wrong number on the protractor?
faq.a: A protractor has two scales — an inner and an outer set of numbers — and children often read the wrong one. Teach them to count from the 0° their arm lines up on, and to check whether the angle looks acute or obtuse before writing the number.

faq.q: How do I explain a degree to a 9-year-old?
faq.a: A degree measures how much something turns. A full spin is 360°, half a turn is 180°, and a quarter turn — a square corner — is 90°. Comparing every angle to that square corner makes the size easy to judge.

faq.q: What is the difference between an obtuse and a straight angle?
faq.a: A straight angle is a perfectly flat line at exactly 180°. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90° but still bends, so it is between 90° and 180°. If there is any bend at all, it is obtuse, not straight.
